title: NEET Negative Marking: When Guessing Is Actually Worth It
description: NEET's +4/-1 marking scheme makes guessing a math problem, not a gut call. Here's the actual expected-value math behind when to guess and when to leave a question blank.
author: Studyloaf Team

content.body: Every NEET aspirant has heard the same advice: "don't guess, negative marking will kill your score." It's repeated so often that most students treat any unfamiliar question as an automatic skip. But NEET's marking scheme isn't a blanket punishment for guessing. It's +4 for a correct answer, -1 for a wrong one, and 0 for leaving it blank. That's a specific set of numbers, and specific numbers mean there's an actual answer to "should I guess here," not a vibe.

content.heading: The math behind a blind guess
content.body: Say you have zero idea about a question, but you can pick from 4 options at random. Your chance of being right is 1/4, and your chance of being wrong is 3/4. The expected value of guessing is:

A completely blind, uniformly random guess on a 4-option question is worth +0.25 marks on average — better than the 0 you get from leaving it blank. This surprises most students, because "negative marking" sounds like it should make blind guessing a loss. It doesn't, as long as you're genuinely picking among all 4 options with no bias.

content.heading: Where the breakeven point actually is
content.body: The real threshold isn't "do I know the answer," it's "is my chance of being right above 20%." Setting the expected value to zero and solving for your probability of being correct, p, shows exactly where guessing stops paying off:

Above a 20% chance of being right, guessing has positive expected value. Below it, guessing costs you marks on average. A pure random guess among 4 options sits at 25%, just above breakeven — which is why it's technically worth it. But this is also why eliminating even one obviously wrong option matters so much: it pushes your odds from 25% to 33%, moving you well clear of the danger zone, not just marginally better.

content.heading: The common mistake this reveals
content.body: The mistake isn't guessing too much. It's treating "I've eliminated 1 of 4 options" and "I have absolutely no idea" as the same situation. If you can rule out even one wrong option, you're at a 33% chance and the expected value jumps to (1/3 × 4) + (2/3 × -1) ≈ +0.67 — more than double a blind guess's +0.25. The advice to "be careful with negative marking" should really only apply to questions where your gut instinct is actively unreliable, for example a topic riddled with lookalike distractor options designed to trap a specific misconception. On those, your real chance of being right can drop below 20%, and that's the case where skipping is genuinely the better call.

content.heading: Turning this into exam behavior
content.body: In practice: never leave a question blank once you've eliminated at least one option, always attempt questions you're even moderately confident about, and reserve blank answers for questions where you have truly no starting point at all — not just questions that feel unfamiliar at first glance. The only way to know which category a question actually falls into is to practice enough of them that your gut sense of "do I know this" gets calibrated against your real hit rate, not your confidence.
